\begin{document}

\title{Structurally Valid, Semantically Wrong:\\Measuring the Unenforced-Rule Gap at a Web Application's Input Boundary}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Zahid Rahimoon}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Independent Researcher} \\
Email: \texttt{zahidrahimoon22@gmail.com}}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A web application's schema validation checks that an input is well formed. It does not check the
business rules that decide whether the input is appropriate, and in the application studied here most
of those rules are not enforced in code. This paper measures how often inputs that pass validation
break such rules, and whether inputs written by large language models (LLMs) differ from inputs
produced in other ways. A Next.js testbed with an enumerated reference of 43 business rules received
\R{e1.inputs} inputs through its real HTTP validation path, from seven generation conditions covering
LLM, random, adversarial, boundary and reference inputs. Semantic validity was decided by deterministic rule functions for objectively decidable rules and by
an independent judge model for the rest. Three results do not depend on the judge. Rules the
application could enforce in code were broken by \R{s.llm.objective}\,\% of structurally valid LLM
inputs, and by \R{s.llm.objnodates}\,\% once a date target driven by a prompt artefact is removed,
below the pre-registered bound. Random structurally valid inputs broke rules more often than LLM
inputs (\R{c.B.rate}\,\% against \R{h1.rate}\,\%), so the gap belongs to the unenforced boundary
rather than to AI writers. And a rule layer costs at most \R{e4.R.c8.maxadd}\,ms of p97.5 latency
against seconds per request for an LLM judge, which saturates at eight concurrent clients. Results
resting on judgement rules are exploratory: calibrated against designed conditions the judge caught
\R{cal.recall}\,\% of planted violations but flagged \R{cal.fpr}\,\% of valid inputs. No candidate
layer reached the pre-registered target of 70\,\% recall at a 5\,\% false-positive rate. The study
covers one application and CPU-only open models.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
input validation, business logic, large language models, web applications, software testing,
empirical study
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

A web application accepts an input only after it passes validation. In the JavaScript and TypeScript
ecosystem that validation is usually a schema: a declarative object stating the type, presence, length,
pattern, numeric range, enumeration and format of every field, checked on the client, again on the
server, and finally by database constraints. Schemas of this kind are well
understood~\cite{pezoa2016foundations,attouche2023jsonschema} and have been studied empirically at
scale~\cite{baazizi2021usagenot}. Other rules depend on what the application is for: a promotional code
has to apply to the item being bought, a workshop cannot start in the past, a review is supposed to be
about the workshop it is attached to. Some can be written as custom refinements, though in practice
most are never written down. The distinction that matters is between the business rules an application
enforces and the many it leaves unenforced.

That limitation is not new: Felmetsger et al.\ separated input-validation flaws, which admit a
general specification, from logic vulnerabilities, which do not~\cite{felmetsger2010waler}, and later
work detected such flaws from behavioural traces, validation mismatches and over-permissive
payloads~\cite{pellegrino2014logicflaws,bisht2010notamper,corradini2023massassignment}. What has
changed is who writes the input. Large language models (LLMs) now fill forms, operate web applications
on a user's behalf, and generate test data~\cite{li2026webformtest,alian2024formnexus,li2025formfactory}.

Recent work shows that LLM output which satisfies a schema is often wrong in meaning. Schema validity
runs well ahead of semantic success for ordering agents, constrained decoders, tool interfaces and
enterprise workflow
generators~\cite{li2026orderbench,ray2026constrainttax,singh2026sob,sigdel2026schemafirst,wrenn2026enterprise}.
All of this concerns model outputs that a tool, an API or a renderer consumes, and there a wrong value
is discarded. At the input boundary of a web application the accepted value is stored and later shown
to other users or to an assistant, and two questions remain open there. How often do LLM-written inputs that pass validation
break the application's business rules? And is that rate different from the rate for other producers of
structurally valid input? Web testing studies cannot answer either, because they treat acceptance by the
application as validity~\cite{li2026webformtest,alian2024formnexus}; one of them notes that incomplete
e-mail addresses may be submitted successfully because the application lacks the
check~\cite{li2026webformtest}, and a robustness study using status codes as its oracle cannot see
failures that return success~\cite{tigulla2026robustness}. Where semantic validity is measured, a base
eight-billion-parameter model produces domain-coherent values under a quarter of the
time~\cite{kim2025llamaresttest}, with no non-LLM comparison.

This paper measures that gap at the input boundary of one purpose-built application with an explicit
rule reference, and compares LLM inputs against random, rule-based, boundary and reference inputs on
the same outcome. I found no prior study that measures semantic validity at a web application's input
boundary against an enumerated rule reference, compares LLM producers with non-LLM producers on that
outcome, or reports what a semantic validation layer costs in the request path on commodity hardware.
The study establishes five things.

\begin{tightitemize}
  \item \textbf{F1. Inputs that the application accepts break rules it does not enforce, and the
  effect is measurable without any model in the loop.} Rules decidable by code alone were broken by
  \R{s.llm.objective}\,\% of structurally valid model inputs and \R{s.B.objective}\,\% of random ones.
  \item \textbf{F2. The gap belongs to the validation boundary, not to AI writers.} Random
  structurally valid inputs broke rules more often than model inputs (\R{c.B.rate}\,\% against
  \R{h1.rate}\,\%), and the ordering holds in every sensitivity variant. Any producer that satisfies
  the schema without knowing the rules falls into the gap.
  \item \textbf{F3. A judge model is not yet a usable oracle for this task, and its error is
  measurable.} Calibrated against planted violations and known-valid inputs, the judge caught
  \R{cal.recall}\,\% of violations while flagging \R{cal.fpr}\,\% of valid inputs, which moves the
  judgement-rule estimate from \R{cal.obs}\,\% to \R{cal.corrected}\,\% once corrected. The
  calibration design itself transfers to any study that uses a model as ground truth.
  \item \textbf{F4. No cheap validation layer closes the gap.} Of six designs evaluated at a bounded
  false-positive rate on held-out fields, the best reached \R{e3.HYB.recall}\,\% recall, most of what
  it caught were violations a line of code could have enforced, and training a classifier on the same
  embeddings did not help (\R{e3.trained.recall}\,\%).
  \item \textbf{F5. On commodity hardware the cost ordering is decisive.} A rule layer adds at most
  \R{e4.R.c8.maxadd}\,ms to p97.5 latency, an embedding layer
  \R{e4.EMB.c1.minadd} to \R{e4.EMB.c1.maxadd}\,ms, and an LLM judge seconds per request, saturating on
  two of three endpoints at eight concurrent clients. The guardrail literature I reviewed reports no
  comparable CPU figures~\cite{jacob2025promptshield,ahmed2026reflexguard,saleem2026layered,wang2026sokguardrails}.
\end{tightitemize}

The testbed, harness, rule reference, raw data and analysis scripts are released, including the
defects found during execution and how each was handled.

\section{Background and Terminology}
\label{sec:background}

\textbf{Structural validation} is every check the application performs before business logic: the
runtime schema (type, presence, length, pattern, range, enumeration, format and any refinements written
into it), service-level checks and database constraints. An input \emph{passes} when the application
accepts it. \textbf{Semantic validity} is whether a structurally valid value is appropriate for the
application's purpose, covering consistency across fields, domain plausibility, compliance with
business rules and safety for downstream consumers such as an LLM component, operationalised as
satisfying every rule in a frozen, enumerated reference. An input that passes structural validation and
violates at least one rule is \textbf{SV-SI} (structurally valid, semantically invalid). The
\emph{conditional} SV-SI rate, the primary outcome, is the share of SV-SI inputs among the structurally
valid inputs whose rules were all decided; without conditioning, a generator that produces more
well-formed values would look worse merely by passing more often.

Terminology differs across communities. The OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet separates syntactic from
semantic validation~\cite{owasp2026inputvalidation}; I count a range the developer wrote into the schema
as structural, because the application enforces it. Security research speaks of logic or business logic
vulnerabilities~\cite{felmetsger2010waler,pellegrino2014logicflaws,metin2025blv} and API testing of
inter-parameter dependencies~\cite{martinlopez2022idl,martinlopez2019catalogue}. In LLM security the
adjective usually means adversarial intent~\cite{singh2026injectioninteraction}, whereas my usage
concerns whether the data is appropriate, which includes that case.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\textbf{Limits of structural validation.} JSON Schema has a formal semantics and a known
complexity~\cite{pezoa2016foundations,attouche2023jsonschema}, and empirical studies describe which
constraints practitioners encode~\cite{baazizi2021usagenot}. Inter-parameter dependencies such as
\emph{requires}, \emph{only-one} and arithmetic relations cannot be stated in an OpenAPI
document~\cite{martinlopez2022idl,martinlopez2019catalogue}, and schema-derived fuzzers inherit the
same boundary~\cite{hatfielddodds2021schemathesis}, and surveys of input-validation vulnerabilities
remain organised around injection classes~\cite{fadlalla2023inputvalidation}. The rules beyond that
boundary are the classical subject of logic-flaw research. Waler inferred likely invariants over
session state and database query parameters and model-checked them~\cite{felmetsger2010waler}, and
related classes are detected by behavioural patterns~\cite{pellegrino2014logicflaws}, parameter
tampering~\cite{bisht2010notamper}, mass-assignment testing~\cite{corradini2023massassignment} and
excessive-data-exposure fuzzing~\cite{pan2024edefuzz}. Recent work applies LLMs to find such flaws in code~\cite{metin2025blv}. In the studies I reviewed the
inputs are crafted by an attacker or a tester, and they are not compared across producers.

\textbf{LLM-generated inputs and schema-valid outputs.} LLMs are better than random and type-based generators at producing inputs that applications accept:
on thirty real forms an LLM-driven approach reaches a passing rate of 83\,\% against 23\,\% for a
static type-based generator and 3\,\% for random crawling~\cite{alian2024formnexus}, and across 146
forms the best of eleven models submits over 98\,\% of its inputs~\cite{li2026webformtest}. The oracle
in both cases is acceptance by the application. Where semantic validity is measured separately, a base
model reaches 22.9\,\% domain-coherent values against 72.4\,\% after
fine-tuning~\cite{kim2025llamaresttest}; related work mines input constraints from specifications and
benchmarks form-filling agents~\cite{li2025formfactory}. For model \emph{outputs}, several 2026
studies document the same pattern, separating schema validity from semantic success and finding the
second well
behind~\cite{li2026orderbench,ray2026constrainttax,singh2026sob,sigdel2026schemafirst,wrenn2026enterprise},
while tool-use benchmarks evaluate emitted calls against a task's expected
answer~\cite{yu2026wildtoolbench,yu2026parambench}. In all of them the semantic check is the oracle
rather than a layer that is itself evaluated.

\textbf{Data validation beyond schemas, and inappropriate input as a security problem.} Data-management research validates data beyond structural schemas with anomaly detection for
machine-learning pipelines~\cite{polyzotis2019datavalidation}, declarative constraint checks that act
as unit tests for data~\cite{schelter2018deequ} and learned detection of column semantic
types~\cite{hulsebos2019sherlock}, all on datasets in batch rather than on one request. Classifying a
single field entry from a context embedding and statistics of recent entries appears in a
patent~\cite{banerjee2025contextembedding}, of which my EMB design is a simpler relative. On the
security side, indirect prompt injection established that models do not separate data from
instructions~\cite{greshake2023indirect} and that attacks on deployed applications
succeed~\cite{kaya2026chatbotplugins}; prompt fragments entered through an ordinary form field can
later drive a database write~\cite{pedro2025p2sql}, the pattern occurs in the
wild~\cite{khodayari2026ipiwild}, and benchmarks extend the coverage~\cite{yi2025bipia,evtimov2025wasp}.
Those inputs are attacker-crafted and mostly free text.

\textbf{Detection layers and their cost.} Input-side detectors include fine-tuned
classifiers~\cite{jacob2025promptshield}, embedding
classifiers~\cite{ayub2024embedding,ahmed2026reflexguard}, small
transformers~\cite{datta2025javelinguard} and LLM judges~\cite{rebedea2023nemo}, and what constrains
deployment is the false-positive rate on benign traffic~\cite{li2024injecguard}. Cost evidence is thin
and tied to GPUs: a detector presented as deployable gives no timing at
all~\cite{jacob2025promptshield}, an embedding guardrail puts its embedding floor at 35\,ms on a
datacentre GPU~\cite{ahmed2026reflexguard}, and a layered framework reports a 61\,ms median on an A100
with model inference excluded~\cite{saleem2026layered}. A systematisation notes that cost and utility
are routinely overlooked~\cite{wang2026sokguardrails}, the one study comparing regex, classifier and
LLM tiers head to head does not state its hardware~\cite{maiorano2026tradeoffs}, and LLM judges can
themselves be redirected by the content they assess~\cite{shi2024judgeattack}. I found no measurement
of a validator for data appropriateness on structured request payloads on CPU.

\textbf{Position of this work.} Three lines of work come closest, and this study differs from each in
one specific way. The output-side studies measure values a model
emits~\cite{li2026orderbench,ray2026constrainttax,singh2026sob,wrenn2026enterprise}, judged against a
task's expected answer; I measure values an application accepts and stores, where nothing raises an
error and the value is later read by people or by an assistant. The form and API testing studies count
acceptance by the application~\cite{alian2024formnexus,li2026webformtest}, so an inappropriate value
that is accepted counts as a success, and the one study that measures domain coherence separately has
no non-LLM comparison~\cite{kim2025llamaresttest}. The guardrail studies evaluate detectors for
adversarial intent and report cost, if at all, on datacentre
GPUs~\cite{ahmed2026reflexguard,saleem2026layered}; I evaluate detectors for ordinary data
appropriateness on structured payloads on a four-core CPU, and report detection quality and cost
together. The comparison across seven producers, including non-LLM ones, is what lets me ask whether
the gap belongs to AI writers or to the validation boundary itself.

\section{Research Questions and Hypotheses}
\label{sec:rq}

The following were frozen, with the primary metrics and the analysis plan, before any experimental
input was generated. Prompt family P5 (injection, Section~\ref{sec:method}) is excluded from all
primary rates and analysed separately.

\begin{tightitemize}
  \item \textbf{RQ1.} Do LLM-generated inputs pass structural validation while violating business
  rules? \emph{H1:} the conditional SV-SI rate of the LLM conditions has a 95\,\% Wilson interval whose
  lower bound exceeds 0.05.
  \item \textbf{RQ2.} How does this vary across field categories? \emph{H2:} rates differ across
  categories; free text and cross-field highest, simple scalar and structured (enumeration) lowest.
  \item \textbf{RQ3.} How do LLM inputs compare with other producers? \emph{H3a:} LLM with field
  context exceeds random; \emph{H3b:} LLM with field context exceeds benign-unusual reference inputs;
  \emph{H3c:} LLM without field context exceeds random.
  \item \textbf{RQ4.} Which violation types dominate? Exploratory.
  \item \textbf{RQ5.} Can an added semantic layer detect SV-SI inputs? \emph{H5:} at least one
  non-judge design reaches recall $\geq 0.70$ at a false-positive rate (FPR) $\leq 0.05$ on held-out
  fields.
  \item \textbf{RQ6.} What does it cost? \emph{H6:} rule and embedding designs add at most 50\,ms to
  p95 request latency while an LLM judge adds at least 1000\,ms.
\end{tightitemize}

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\textbf{Subject under study.} The subject is a purpose-built Next.js~16 application written in TypeScript. It uses Zod~4 for
validation on the client and the server, Prisma with SQLite for persistence, and a local Ollama runtime
for two AI-facing features, support-ticket triage and a booking assistant. It has seven input surfaces and 39 fields. A reference file enumerates 43 business rules, of which
five are enforced in code, two of those as Zod refinements (a birth date not in the future, a workshop
end after its start); the remaining 38 are unenforced, a profile chosen to resemble small production
applications. Each rule is classified in advance as objective, decidable from the input, the database
and the clock (19 rules), or judgement (24 rules). The application and the rule reference were tagged
before any input was generated (commit \texttt{62a7267}), and the commit is recorded with every run. A
purpose-built subject is a deliberate trade: real applications do not enumerate their business rules,
and without a complete reference the semantic outcome has no ground truth.

\textbf{Targets and generation conditions.} Seventeen targets covering 22 fields represent every field category, every directly AI-facing field,
and five cross-field pairs whose rule relates the two members; each carries a purpose description, its
rule identifiers and its structural constraints. Seven conditions produce values for each target: \textbf{A} valid reference values; \textbf{B} random values that satisfy the
schema, from a seeded generator of word sequences, numbers and dates within the schema's limits, with no
attempt at meaning; \textbf{C} rule-based adversarial values, one template per unenforced rule;
\textbf{D} an LLM given the field name and the structural constraints only; \textbf{E} the same LLM
given the field's purpose and rules as well; \textbf{F} boundary values at the schema edges; and
\textbf{G} benign but unusual reference values. Conditions A and G were specified as human-written. Their \R{e1.refdrafted} values were first
drafted with the help of a language model and checked against the schemas and the objective rules.
\ifreviewed I then went through every value myself, kept \R{review.keep}, replaced \R{review.change}
and deleted \R{review.delete}. The application rejected all \R{review.change} replacements, which were
promotional codes it does not recognise, so these conditions rest on the kept values and I call them
human-curated rather than human-written.\else The researcher's review of them is outstanding
(Section~\ref{sec:threats}).\fi

\textbf{LLM generation.} Conditions D and E use qwen3:4b (Q4\_K\_M) through Ollama on a four-core CPU, at temperature 0.8,
nucleus 0.9, with a fixed seed per run, three runs, and five values per call. Seven prompt families are
stored as hashed files: P1 legitimate values, P2 unusual values, P3 values that satisfy the constraints
but ``would be wrong for the application to accept'', P4 values whose meaning depends on downstream
interpretation, P5 injection for AI-facing targets only, P6 boundary values, and P7 Unicode variants.
Because P3 asks for violations, results are reported per family as well as pooled. The model
identifier, digest, temperature, seed, prompt file and prompt hash are recorded for every value, and
failed calls were counted and never regenerated: \R{e1.failrecords} failure records in
\R{e1.failcells} prompt cells, \R{e1.failcallerror} of them call errors such as calls aborted at the
120\,s timeout and \R{e1.failunparse} unparseable replies. A further \R{e1.keymismatch} generated
values used key names other than the target's; a harness defect had filled those keys from the form's
defaults, so the records measure the defaults rather than the model and count as generation failures.

\textbf{Structural measurement.} Each input is measured twice. It is checked against the same schema object the application imports, and
it is submitted over HTTP to the real route handler, which records the status, the service errors and
the time. The structural outcome is the application's own decision, so an input rejected by one of the
five enforced business checks counts as a structural rejection. Booking state is reset to the seed
before each booking request.

\textbf{Semantic ground truth.} Objective rules are decided by rule functions. The 11 objective rules that apply to the 17 targets all
have one. Judgement rules are decided by a judge model from a different family than the generator
(gemma3:4b, temperature 0). The judge sees the field purpose, the rule text and the submitted value of
the target's fields. It never sees the condition, the prompt family or the intent. Seven judgement rules depend on other
fields of the same record, such as capacity being plausible for the location. Those were first judged
without that context and were re-judged with the whole record; the re-judged verdicts are the ones
reported, and a sensitivity analysis drops the seven rules altogether. \ifhumanlabels A human annotator labelled \R{ann.items} structurally valid inputs blind to
condition, with \R{ann.repeats} items repeated to estimate the annotator's consistency. Where a human
verdict exists it takes precedence over the judge.\else A planned human annotation of 200 inputs, which
would validate the judge, has not been completed.\fi{} An input is \emph{decided} when every applicable
rule has a verdict. For compute reasons the judge was applied to a stratified sample: \R{judge.base}
structurally valid inputs drawn round-robin across target and condition with a fixed seed, plus
\R{judge.supplement} inputs for two booking targets that were re-measured after a defect
(Section~\ref{sec:threats}), up to 14 per stratum and as many as were available.

\textbf{Analysis population and statistics.} Of the \R{e1.inputs} inputs, the following are excluded: \R{e1.keymismatch} key-mismatch records,
\R{e1.retried} records produced by inadvertent retries of failed calls, \R{e1.p5} injection-family
inputs, and\ifreviewed{} \R{e1.reviewexcluded} reference values that the reviewer deleted or
replaced\else{} no reviewer exclusions\fi. That leaves \R{e1.primary} inputs. Of these, \R{e1.passes}
passed structural validation and \R{e1.decided} are decided. The remaining passes were either not in
the judge sample (\R{e1.undecided.unjudged}) or received no usable verdict
(\R{e1.undecided.unsure}). Rates carry Wilson 95\,\% confidence intervals (CIs) and contrasts are reported as odds ratios
(ORs). H1 is evaluated on the lower bound of its interval, H2 with a $\chi^2$ test and Cram\'er's $V$,
and H3a to H3c with three one-sided Fisher tests under Holm correction. The judge sample gives the
conditions different target mixes, so each contrast is also tested within target with the
Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test, added after data collection. Values generated in one call, and
targets within a category, are not independent, so Wilson intervals are too narrow; every main rate and
contrast therefore also carries a cluster bootstrap interval (2000 draws over \R{cb.calls} generation
calls and, separately, \R{cb.targets} targets). Every other analysis is labelled exploratory. It was
fixed in advance that if judge-human agreement on judgement rules falls below $\kappa=0.4$, every
result depending on those rules is reported as exploratory. Every number here is generated from the raw
data by released scripts. The hypotheses, metrics and analysis plan were fixed in a dated decision log
before generation began and are released unchanged; version control over the analysis code started
after data collection, so that log and the frozen subject tag are the evidence of pre-registration,
not a commit history.

\section{Semantic Validation Layers}
\label{sec:layer}

Six designs run as a drop-in check after structural validation. \textbf{R} packages the objective
rule functions; because those also define the ground truth for objective rules, R cannot produce a
false positive on them, so it is a floor rather than a competitor. \textbf{EMB} scores a
value by its cosine distance from an embedding (nomic-embed-text) of the field's purpose and rules,
using no labelled examples; \textbf{EMB-TRAINED} fits logistic regression on those same embeddings over
the training folds, which is the design the frozen plan anticipated. \textbf{SLM} prompts a small
language model (SLM; qwen3:1.7b) with the field purpose and rules for a verdict and a confidence.
\textbf{HYB} runs R first and then EMB on what R passes. \textbf{JUDGE} sends the same prompt to
qwen3:4b, the generator's model, as a reference point, so SLM and JUDGE receive a rubric similar to the
ground-truth judge's. The prompted designs run at temperature 0, and a reply without a verdict counts
as a pass, because the deployed layer fails open.

Evaluation is leave-fields-out over five folds. In each fold the threshold is the smallest score at
which at most 5\,\% of the valid training-fold inputs are flagged, and that threshold is applied to the
held-out fields. Designs are compared on recall at that operating point, with FPR, precision and the
threshold-free area under the ROC curve (AUROC). The model-based designs were scored on a stratified
sample of \R{e3.n} decided inputs, of which \R{e3.pos} are SV-SI, and all designs are compared on that
sample; the fast designs were also scored on all \R{e3.fulln} decided inputs, a population that
includes the injection family and the retried records.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\textbf{Rate of semantic violations (RQ1).} \IfFileExists{tables/tab_conditions.tex}{\input{tables/tab_conditions}}{}

Among decided, structurally valid LLM inputs, \R{h1.k} of \R{h1.n} (\R{h1.rate}\,\%, 95\,\% CI
\R{h1.ci}) broke at least one business rule (Table~\ref{tab:conditions}), so H1 is supported. The
pooled rate includes prompt family P3, which asks for rule violations; without P3 it is
\R{s.llm.nopthree}\,\%. By family the rate ranges from \R{fam.P1.DE}\,\% for legitimate-value
prompts to \R{fam.P3.DE}\,\% when violations are requested, with context-dependent
(\R{fam.P4.DE}\,\%), unusual (\R{fam.P2.DE}\,\%), Unicode-variation (\R{fam.P7.DE}\,\%) and
boundary (\R{fam.P6.DE}\,\%) prompts in between. Every family is above the pre-registered bound.
\ifjudgeweak Agreement between the judge and the human annotator is below the pre-registered
threshold (``How good is the ground truth?'' below), so every rate depending on judgement rules is
exploratory, this one included; the objective-rule rate depends only on the rule functions.\fi{}
The rate survives most sensitivity variants in Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}, including objective rules
alone (\R{s.llm.objective}\,\%, CI \R{s.llm.objective.ci}). It does not survive the strictest one.
One target dominates the objective violations: on workshop dates (F15+F16) nearly every model value
was in the past, because the prompts never state the current date, a property of the harness rather
than of the application. Removing both the judge and that target leaves \R{s.llm.objnodates}\,\% (CI
\R{s.llm.objnodates.ci}), whose lower bound is below the 0.05 threshold, \textbf{so H1 is not
supported on the one variant that depends neither on the judge nor on the date artefact}. H1 is
supported as pre-registered and not supported on judge-independent evidence alone. Per run the rate was \R{run.D.1}, \R{run.D.2} and \R{run.D.3}\,\% without field context and
\R{run.E.1}, \R{run.E.2} and \R{run.E.3}\,\% with it; including the retried records gives
\R{h1.withretried}\,\%. The reference conditions bound the labelling from both sides: \R{c.A.rate}\,\%
of valid inputs were labelled invalid and \R{c.C.rate}\,\% of adversarial ones were caught.

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_sensitivity.tex}{\input{tables/tab_sensitivity}}{}

\textbf{Field categories (RQ2).} 
Rates differ across categories, but H2 is counted as \emph{not supported}: its directional prediction was that simple scalar and structured fields would be lowest,
and structured came out highest. The association statistic ($\chi^2(6)=\R{h2.chi}$, Cram\'er's
$V=\R{h2.v}$) is reported descriptively only, because with one to four targets per category it tests
heterogeneity between targets rather than between categories.\ifjudgeweak{} These rates also rest on
judgement rules, so they are exploratory.\fi{} The pattern is as follows. Free text (\R{cat.freetext}\,\%) and
cross-field (\R{cat.crossfield}\,\%) are high, as expected, structured fields are the highest
(\R{cat.structured}\,\%) rather than among the lowest, and financial fields are the lowest
(\R{cat.financial}\,\%); AI-facing is \R{cat.aifacing}\,\%, search \R{cat.search}\,\% and
simple scalar \R{cat.simple}\,\%. Categories contain between one and four targets, and per-category
and per-target tables are in the repository. The
structured category is a single target, a ticket's priority and category. The calibration below shows
that the judge flagged \R{cal.worstfp} of \R{cal.worstn} valid inputs on one of that target's rules
(\R{cal.worstrule}) even when given the whole record, so the reversal is a property of that rule's
labelling rather than of enumerated fields in general.

\textbf{Comparison of producers (RQ3).} \IfFileExists{tables/tab_contrasts.tex}{\input{tables/tab_contrasts}}{}

None of the three pre-registered contrasts is supported, and two point the other way
(Table~\ref{tab:contrasts}).\ifjudgeweak{} They are computed on labels that include judgement rules, so under the
agreement gate they are exploratory as well. The objective-rule sensitivity row shows the same
direction without the judge.\fi{} Random structurally valid inputs broke rules in \R{c.B.rate}\,\% of
cases, more often than LLM inputs without field context (\R{c.D.rate}\,\%) or with it
(\R{c.E.rate}\,\%), and that holds in every sensitivity variant (Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}).
Clustering changes how firm each contrast is. Resampling whole targets, the difference between
context-aware model inputs and random inputs still excludes zero (\R{cb.dH3aEB.target}), while the
difference between context-free model inputs and random inputs does not (\R{cb.dH3cDB.target}), and
the pooled LLM rate has a target-clustered interval of \R{cb.llm.target}, far wider than its Wilson
interval. Within
target (CMH, post hoc) the odds of a violation were lower for LLM inputs with context than for random
inputs (odds ratio \R{cmh.EvB.or}, 95\,\% CI \R{cmh.EvB.ci}) and lower without context
(\R{cmh.DvB.or}, \R{cmh.DvB.ci}); adversarial inputs exceeded random ones (\R{cmh.CvB.or},
\R{cmh.CvB.ci}), and field context lowered the odds relative to the schema alone (\R{cmh.EvD.or},
\R{cmh.EvD.ci}). Condition E is given the very rules that define the outcome, so that reduction is an
upper bound on what context can achieve rather than a deployable intervention: an application able to
put its rules in a prompt can also enforce the objective ones in code. H3b is the one contrast that points the way it was predicted to, and it does not reach the
threshold: LLM inputs with field context broke rules more often than benign-unusual reference inputs,
but not detectably so when pooled ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=\R{h3.EgtG.pholm}$), only borderline within
target (\R{cmh.EvG.or}, \R{cmh.EvG.ci}, \R{cmh.EvG.p}), and resampling whole targets puts the
difference at \R{cb.dH3bEG.target} percentage points, which includes zero. \ifreviewed The reference
inputs are also AI-drafted values curated by a human reviewer, so this compares model input with
human-curated input rather than with input a person wrote unaided.\else The reference inputs are
AI-drafted, so this is not an AI-versus-human result.\fi{}

An exploratory variation repeated conditions D and E on ten targets with families P1 to P4, changing
only the generator. The 1.7-billion-parameter model produced more violations than the 4-billion model
on objective rules (\R{e2b.small.obj}\,\% against \R{e2b.ref.obj}\,\%, OR \R{e2b.small.obj.or},
\R{e2b.small.obj.p}) and on all rules (\R{e2b.small.all}\,\% against \R{e2b.ref.all}\,\%,
\R{e2b.small.all.p}); neither the 8-billion model (\R{e2b.large.all}\,\%) nor temperature 0
(\R{e2b.tzero.all}\,\%) differed detectably. With one run per generator this only indicates that a
smaller model may widen the gap.


\textbf{Violation types (RQ4).} \ifjudgeweak Counts of judgement-rule violations depend on the judge and are exploratory.\fi{}
Judgement-rule violations outnumber objective ones (\R{viol.jud} against \R{viol.obj}, across all
conditions). The single most frequent violation is objective: a workshop must start in the future
(\R{rule.B-CO-2} violations). The next two, the ticket priority rule (\R{rule.B-TK-4}) and the capacity
rule (\R{rule.B-CO-7}), are the two rules the calibration below shows the judge cannot decide, so
those counts measure judge behaviour as much as violation. A profile bio addressed to the assistant
(\R{rule.B-PR-6}) and duration plausibility (\R{rule.B-CO-3}) follow. On AI-facing fields,
\R{ai.llm.svsi} structurally valid LLM inputs violated a rule. Of those, \R{ai.llm.p5} came from the
injection family and \R{ai.llm.nonp5} from the other prompt families.

\textbf{How good is the ground truth?} Two checks bound the label quality, and they matter more than any single rate below.

\emph{Calibration against the designed conditions.} Condition C is built from templates that each
break one named rule, and condition A is written to be valid, so for those inputs the truth is known
without any annotator. On judgement rules the judge caught \R{cal.caught} of \R{cal.designed} designed
violations (recall \R{cal.recall}\,\%, CI \R{cal.recall.ci}) and flagged \R{cal.fp} of \R{cal.validn}
valid inputs (false-positive rate \R{cal.fpr}\,\%, CI \R{cal.fpr.ci}). Per-rule figures are in
Table~\ref{tab:calibration}. A false-positive rate of that size matters, because the observed
judgement-rule rate among model inputs is only \R{cal.obs}\,\%: correcting it for the measured recall
and false-positive rate gives \R{cal.corrected}\,\%. Condition C is deliberately blatant, so its
recall is optimistic and the corrected figure is a lower bound, but the gap between
\R{cal.obs}\,\% and \R{cal.corrected}\,\% attributes about \R{cal.errorshare}\,\% of the
judgement-rule signal in this study to judge error rather than to violation. The error is concentrated:
\R{cal.nfprules} of the \R{cal.rules} calibrated rules produced any false positive at all, and the
worst, \R{cal.worstrule}, fired on \R{cal.worstfp} of \R{cal.worstn} valid inputs even when the judge
was given the whole record.

\emph{Agreement with a human.}\ifhumanlabels{} On judgement rules the judge agreed with the annotator
on \R{agree.judge}\,\% of \R{n.judge} verdicts (Cohen's $\kappa=\R{kappa.judge}$), and the annotator
was unsure on \R{unsure.judge}\,\%. \ifjudgeweak Agreement is below the pre-registered 0.4, so every
judgement-rule result in this paper is exploratory.\fi{} That annotation cannot settle which rater is
at fault, because the same annotator also disagreed with the deterministic rule functions on objective
rules (\R{agree.rules}\,\% agreement, $\kappa=\R{kappa.rules}$, \R{fail.other.rules} rule-function
violations against \R{fail.human.rules}), and those rules are decidable by code. A single annotator
working at \R{ann.median_s}\,s per item is therefore not an adequate reference, which is why the
calibration above carries the argument instead. The annotator was self-consistent on repeated items
($\kappa=\R{kappa.self}$).\else{} The human annotation was not completed.\fi

\IfFileExists{tables/tab_calibration.tex}{\input{tables/tab_calibration}}{}

\textbf{Detection quality (RQ5).} \IfFileExists{tables/tab_detection.tex}{\input{tables/tab_detection}}{}

No design reached the target, so H5 is not supported (Table~\ref{tab:detection}).\ifjudgeweak{}
Detection is measured against the same labels, so the judgement-rule part of these results is
exploratory as well. The objective-rule part is not.\fi{} At the operating point fixed on the training
folds, the best non-judge design, HYB, detected \R{e3.HYB.recall}\,\% of SV-SI inputs (CI
\R{e3.HYB.ci}) at a held-out FPR of \R{e3.HYB.fpr}\,\%, which is above the 5\,\% it was tuned for. Most
of what it catches comes from R. HYB and R both caught \R{e3.HYB.robj}\,\% of the inputs that violate
only objective rules, and \R{e3.HYB.rjud}\,\% and \R{e3.R.rjud}\,\% of those that violate a judgement
rule. On all decided inputs the fast designs reach \R{e3.R.fullrecall}\,\% for R and
\R{e3.HYB.fullrecall}\,\% for HYB. EMB on its own was no better than chance (AUROC
\R{e3.EMB.auroc}).

The prompted designs rank inputs better (AUROC \R{e3.SLM.auroc} for SLM and \R{e3.JUDGE.auroc} for
JUDGE against \R{e3.HYB.auroc} for HYB), but their scores take only a handful of values, so holding FPR
to 5\,\% on the training fields forces the threshold to the top confidence level, where SLM detects
\R{e3.SLM.recall}\,\% and JUDGE \R{e3.JUDGE.recall}\,\%. Taking each model's own verdict without
tuning, which is exploratory, SLM detects \R{e3.SLM.nrecall}\,\% while flagging \R{e3.SLM.nfpr}\,\% of
valid inputs, and JUDGE detects \R{e3.JUDGE.nrecall}\,\% while flagging \R{e3.JUDGE.nfpr}\,\% and
gives no usable verdict for \R{e3.JUDGE.noverdict}\,\% of inputs. Both receive a rubric similar to the
ground-truth judge's, so on judgement rules their measured ``recall'' is largely agreement between
small language models and the small model that produced the labels, not detection of violations, and
R's recall on objective rules is tautological because the same rule functions decide the labels.
The frozen plan anticipated a \emph{trained} classifier, and the leave-fields-out labels support one:
logistic regression on the same embeddings, fitted on the training folds, reaches
\R{e3.trained.recall}\,\% recall (CI \R{e3.trained.ci}) at \R{e3.trained.fpr}\,\% FPR over
\R{e3.trained.n} inputs, with AUROC \R{e3.trained.auroc}. Training does not rescue the embedding
design. Thresholds also did not transfer across fields: the held-out FPR per fold reached
\R{e3.emb.foldfprmax}\,\% for the embedding-based designs.

\textbf{Overhead (RQ6).} \IfFileExists{tables/tab_e4.tex}{\input{tables/tab_e4}}{}

Each configuration ran against the production build with only its own model loaded, and no request
or layer call failed in any run (Table~\ref{tab:e4}). H6 is not supported, because its first part
fails. R added at most \R{e4.R.c1.maxadd}\,ms to p97.5 latency with one client and
\R{e4.R.c8.maxadd}\,ms with eight, within the 50\,ms bound; the negative differences at eight clients
reflect run-to-run variation. EMB added
\R{e4.EMB.c1.minadd} to \R{e4.EMB.c1.maxadd}\,ms with one client, above the bound, and
\R{e4.EMB.c8.minadd} to \R{e4.EMB.c8.maxadd}\,ms with eight, because every request embeds its text on the
same CPU. On the p95 bracket used as a sensitivity check, EMB fails on the review endpoint and is undetermined
on the other two. The second part of H6 holds. SLM added
\R{e4.SLM.c1.minp50add} to \R{e4.SLM.c1.maxp50add}\,ms at the median with one client and JUDGE added
\R{e4.JUDGE.c1.minp50add} to \R{e4.JUDGE.c1.maxp50add}\,ms. The model server answers one request at a
time, so requests queue under concurrency. With eight clients SLM added
\R{e4.SLM.c8.minp50add} to \R{e4.SLM.c8.maxp50add}\,ms at the median, and JUDGE completed no request
within the 60\,s window in all three runs on the course endpoint and in two of three on the review
endpoint. Throughput on the course endpoint fell from \R{e4.structural.c1.courses.rps} requests per
second with structural validation alone to \R{e4.SLM.c1.courses.rps} with SLM and
\R{e4.JUDGE.c1.courses.rps} with JUDGE. Set against detection quality, only R and HYB lie on the cost-detection frontier: SLM, JUDGE and EMB
each cost more and detect less than one of them at the pre-registered operating point. The frontier
plot is released with the artefacts.


\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\ifjudgeweak Throughout this section, every statement that rests on judgement rules is exploratory,
because judge-human agreement fell below the pre-registered threshold. Statements about objective
rules do not depend on the judge.\fi

\textbf{RQ1: the gap is measurable, and its size depends on what is asked.} About a third of
structurally valid LLM inputs broke an unenforced rule, which extends output-side
findings~\cite{li2026orderbench,singh2026sob,wrenn2026enterprise} to inputs an application would
store. The magnitude is sensitive to prompt intent, to one date-dependent target, and to the judge, and
the two checks it does not survive matter as much as the headline. The honest summary is that
unenforced rules are broken often enough to matter, that this study does not establish the size of the
effect, and that the ground truth is the limiting factor.

\textbf{RQ2: where it occurs is uneven.} Category is moderately associated with the outcome, but
individual targets drive that association: one target with a clock-dependent rule accounts for over
half of the cross-field violations, and the structured category is a single target on which the
calibration shows the judge is unreliable.

\textbf{RQ3: the gap is not specific to AI.} This is the central negative result. Random values that
satisfy the schema broke rules more often than model values, with or without field context, both pooled
and within target, which points to the validation boundary rather than to the producer. A schema admits
many values the application should reject, and any producer that satisfies the schema without knowing
the rules will supply some of them. What distinguishes the model is that context helps: giving it the
purpose and the rules cut the odds of a violation by \R{cmh.EvD.reduction}\,\% relative to the schema
alone. The random generator makes word sequences with no attempt at meaning, so it bounds the space
rather than representing a person, and the failure of H3a and H3c carries little information by itself.
The comparison that would settle the AI question, model input against input written unaided by several
people, has not been run.

\textbf{RQ4: most violations are ordinary.} The single most frequent violation was of an objective
rule the application could enforce directly, though judgement-rule violations remain the majority. On
AI-facing fields most LLM violations came from ordinary prompts rather than injection attempts, so the
gap is mostly unenforced business logic rather than attack.

\textbf{RQ5: no cheap layer closes it.} The fast designs that can be held to a low FPR, R and HYB,
find about a quarter of the violations, and most of that is objective violations that could simply be
enforced. JUDGE under the same constraint finds \R{e3.JUDGE.recall}\,\%, again mostly objective. The
prompted models rank inputs better than the rest (AUROC \R{e3.JUDGE.auroc} and \R{e3.SLM.auroc}) but
produce coarse, field-dependent scores, so the constraint pushes them to an all-or-nothing threshold;
left at their own decision rule they catch far more while rejecting \R{e3.JUDGE.nfpr}\,\% and
\R{e3.SLM.nfpr}\,\% of valid inputs. Detecting judgement-rule violations remains the open problem.

\textbf{RQ6: cost rises faster than detection.} On commodity CPU hardware only the rule layer is
effectively free, and it detects violations of rules the application could have enforced in the first
place. The embedding layer costs tens of milliseconds and detected almost nothing. The prompted models
cost half a second to several seconds per request with one client, a local model server handles one
request at a time so they cannot keep up with eight, and their better ranking of inputs does not
survive the false-positive constraint. Two caveats bound that. Run-to-run variation at eight clients
reaches the same order as the embedding effect that fails H6 at one client, so the embedding verdict is
marginal; and the serialisation belongs to one local model server, since a hosted judge would cost
roughly a second per call and scale horizontally. On this hardware the practical recommendation is to
enforce objective rules in code and to treat judgement rules as an open problem, rather than to add a
model to the request path.

\textbf{Alternative explanations.} The six explanations fixed in advance fare as follows. \emph{Weak
business rules rather than AI:} consistent with the data, because the gap appears for every producer
that does not know the rules. \emph{Random inputs produce the same effect:} consistent, and random
inputs exceed model inputs. \emph{Unusual human inputs behave the same:} \ifreviewed not resolved. Context-aware model inputs
broke rules somewhat more often than human-curated unusual ones (\R{cmh.EvG.or}, \R{cmh.EvG.ci}), but
the pooled test does not reach the threshold and the target-clustered difference includes
zero\else not tested, because the reference inputs are AI-drafted\fi. \emph{Confined to free
text:} not supported, because structured and cross-field targets also show high rates, although single
targets drive them. \emph{Prompt injection under another name:} not supported. Injection prompts are
excluded from all rates and account for \R{ai.llm.p5} of \R{ai.llm.svsi} LLM violations on AI-facing
fields. \emph{Too expensive to deploy:} supported for the model-based layers on CPU hardware, and not
supported for rules.

\section{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\textbf{Internal validity.} Labelling is the main threat. Judgement rules were decided by one 4B judge
\ifhumanlabels (agreement with a human annotator $\kappa=\R{kappa.judge}$ on \R{n.judge} shared
verdicts, below the pre-registered 0.4, so judgement-rule results are exploratory)\else without human
validation\fi. The calibration shows the re-judge did not make the seven cross-field rules reliable, so the
sensitivity row that drops all seven is still reported: it lowers the LLM rate to
\R{s.llm.nocontext}\,\% and the random rate by more (Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity}), leaving the RQ3
direction intact. Agreement on semantic judgements can be low even between
humans~\cite{calo2026semanticgap}.\ifhumanlabels{} The disagreement here is not
one-sided noise. On the shared verdicts the judge called \R{fail.other.judge} violations against the
annotator's \R{fail.human.judge}, so the judge is the stricter rater and judgement-rule rates may be
too high, and it returned no usable verdict on \R{noverdict.judge} further rules the annotator decided.
The annotator in turn disagreed with the deterministic rule functions on objective rules
($\kappa=\R{kappa.rules}$), which decide such rules from the record and the clock, so part of the low
agreement is annotation error or the limited context the annotator saw rather than judge error
alone.\fi{} The judge sample gives the conditions different target mixes, and target-weighted rates
are close to the pooled ones.
Time-relative rules are evaluated against the clock at the moment the labels are merged, so a later
re-run can change labels near the boundary, and the judge ran once, its run-to-run stability on this
CPU unmeasured.

\textbf{Defects found and corrected.} Eight defects were found during execution, each recorded as a
deviation with the invalid data preserved: the database was not reset between booking measurements, so
capacity ran out and those targets were re-measured; a resume routine retried failed generation calls,
whose records are excluded; model outputs with other key names were silently replaced by form
defaults, and those records are excluded as generation failures; a first overhead run never enabled
the layer and is discarded; the first detector analysis chose thresholds with a quantile, which fails
for coarse scores; the label merge never passed human verdicts to the ground-truth algorithm while the
importer dropped cells after an empty one; the judge was asked to decide seven cross-field rules
without the other fields, so those rules were re-judged with the whole record; and the merge appended
rather than rewrote its output, so re-running it counted every input twice. Each was fixed before any
figure computed from it was reported. Three were found not by my own checking but
by separate adversarial review passes over the code and the analysis outputs, run with LLM reviewers,
and one by a senior academic reviewer reading the draft.

\textbf{External validity.} The study covers one application in one domain, built by the researcher,
with one enforcement profile, so the results may not transfer. Generation uses quantised open models
of 1.7 to 8 billion parameters on CPU; frontier models may behave differently, and evidence that scale
does not predict semantic quality~\cite{singh2026sob,wrenn2026enterprise} cuts both ways. The prompts
never state the current date, which inflates date-rule violations for model inputs.

\textbf{Construct validity.} Semantic invalidity is defined by a frozen reference another team would
write differently. It was frozen before any input existed and violations are reported per rule, so a
reader can discount rules they disagree with.

\textbf{Conclusion validity.} Pooling three runs inflates the LLM sample, and per-run rates are
reported for that reason. The category mapping assigns dual-tagged fields to one category, which was
decided before the data existed but not logged at the time. The three contrasts H3a to H3c were the
only pre-declared ones, but they are computed on labels that include judgement rules,
so\ifjudgeweak{} they too are exploratory under the pre-registered agreement gate, and only results
decided by the rule functions alone remain confirmatory.\else{} they remain confirmatory while the
other contrasts are exploratory.\fi{} \ifreviewed H3b in particular compares model input with
human-curated input, not with input written unaided, because the reference conditions were AI-drafted
before I reviewed them.\else Until the researcher's review is recorded, H3b is exploratory and the
alternative explanation that unusual human inputs behave similarly is untested.\fi

\textbf{Who produced the human data.} \ifhumanlabels I carried out both the review and the
annotation, and I also built the subject application and wrote the rule reference. The annotation is
blind to the generation condition, because the interface never shows it, but it is not independent of
the study, and one annotator cannot establish how far the disagreement with the judge generalises. The
review took \R{review.minutes} minutes for \R{e1.refdrafted} values and the annotation
\R{ann.minutes} minutes for \R{ann.items} items, a median of \R{ann.median_s}\,s per item, both well
below the effort budgeted, which may itself contribute to the low agreement. The per-item answers and
their timestamps are released.\else The human tasks have not been carried out.\fi

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Schema validation answers whether an input is well formed, not whether it belongs. At the input
boundary of one application with an explicit rule reference, structurally valid inputs broke unenforced
business rules often enough to matter, and random inputs broke them more often than model inputs, so
the gap belongs to the boundary rather than to AI writers. How large the gap is remains open: the judge-independent estimate falls below the pre-registered
bound once a prompt artefact is removed, and correcting for the judge's false-positive rate removes
about \R{cal.errorshare}\,\% of the judgement-rule signal. The single most frequent violation was of
an objective rule a line of validation code could enforce,
and none of the candidate layers, trained or untrained, detected the pre-registered share of
violations at a tolerable false-positive rate.\ifjudgeweak{} A human annotation of \R{ann.items}
inputs agreed with the judge only at $\kappa=\R{kappa.judge}$, below the threshold fixed in advance,
so the ground truth for judgement rules is the weakest part of the study.\fi{} On a four-core CPU,
rules added at most \R{e4.R.c8.maxadd}\,ms at p97.5, while at the median a small language model added
about half a second and an LLM judge several seconds, saturating with eight concurrent clients.

Future work should \ifreviewed\else complete the review of the reference conditions, \fi
\ifhumanlabels\else validate the judge against human annotation, \fi strengthen the ground truth with
several annotators and more time per item, replace the rules the calibration shows the judge cannot
decide, collect reference inputs written unaided by several people, and repeat the protocol on an
existing open-source application.
